claim: Pediatric acute respiratory distress syndrome (PARDS) was first defined in children in 2015 as the acute onset of parenchymal lung disease on chest x-ray with severe hypoxemia not explained by cardiac disease.
source: Pediatric acute respiratory distress syndrome (PARDS) was first defined in children in 2015 as the acute onset of parenchymal lung disease on chest x-ray with severe hypoxemia not explained by cardiac disease (Pediatric Acute Lung Injury Consensus Conference Group, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the Pediatric Acute Lung Injury Consensus Conference Group, 2015.

claim: PARDS has lower incidence than adult ARDS (2–13 vs. 17.9–81.0 per 100,000 person-years).
source: PARDS compared to ARDS affecting adults has lower incidence (2–13 Pediatric Acute Lung Injury Consensus Conference Group, 2015; Schouten et al., 2016; Hough, 2017 vs. 17.9–81.0 Rubenfeld et al., 2009 ; Rubenfeld et al., 2009; Li et al., 2011 per 100,000 person-years)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations comparing pediatric and adult ARDS incidence rates.

claim: PARDS has lower mortality than adult ARDS (18%–27% vs. 27%–45%).
source: PARDS compared to ARDS affecting adults has lower incidence (2–13 Pediatric Acute Lung Injury Consensus Conference Group, 2015; Schouten et al., 2016; Hough, 2017 vs. 17.9–81.0 Rubenfeld et al., 2009 ; Rubenfeld et al., 2009; Li et al., 2011 per 100,000 person-years) and mortality (18%–27% Pediatric Acute Lung Injury Consensus Conference Group, 2015 vs. 27%–45% Rubenfeld et al., 2009; Li et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations providing mortality data for pediatric and adult ARDS.

claim: Sepsis is the most common cause of ARDS affecting adults while pneumonia is the most common cause of PARDS.
source: Sepsis is the most common cause of ARDS affecting adults while pneumonia is the most common cause of PARDS (Khemani et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Khemani et al., 2019.

claim: Epidemiologic differences between pediatric and adult ARDS may reflect differences in lung function, immune response, and disease mechanism between children and adults.
source: Epidemiologic differences between pediatric and adult ARDS may reflect differences in lung function, immune response, and disease mechanism between children and adults.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential reasons for observed epidemiologic differences.

claim: Prior studies have noted differences in risk factors and clinical outcomes for children with distinct PARDS phenotypes (e.g., direct vs. indirect lung injury), which may reflect differences in pathobiology.
source: Prior studies have noted differences in risk factors and clinical outcomes for children with distinct PARDS phenotypes (e.g., direct vs. indirect lung injury), which may reflect differences in pathobiology (Yehya et al., 2018; Whitney et al., 2020a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies that documented differences in PARDS phenotypes.

claim: A relatively small proportion of children who are at risk for PARDS after exposure to a severe physiologic insult develop PARDS, which may reflect underlying biological differences in genetically determined host susceptibility.
source: The fact that a relatively small proportion of children, who are at risk for PARDS after exposure to a severe physiologic insult, develop PARDS may reflect underlying biological differences in genetically determined host susceptibility.
evidence: This is an inference about the potential role of genetic susceptibility based on observed patterns.

claim: PARDS mortality has decreased slightly over time, possibly due to improvements in delivery of supportive care.
source: PARDS mortality has decreased slightly over time (Pediatric Acute Lung Injury Consensus Conference Group, 2015; Khemani et al., 2019), possibly due to improvements in delivery of supportive care.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations showing mortality trends, with speculation about the cause.

claim: Targeted pharmacologic therapies for PARDS are lacking, which may reflect a lack of knowledge about the pathobiology of this complex disease process.
source: Targeted pharmacologic therapies are lacking, which may reflect a lack of knowledge about the pathobiology of this complex disease process.
evidence: This is an inference about the relationship between lack of therapies and understanding of pathobiology.

claim: The development of PARDS in response to a severe physiologic insult is thought to reflect epithelial lung injury, systemic inflammation, and activation of the vascular endothelium.
source: The development of PARDS in response to a severe physiologic insult is thought to reflect epithelial lung injury, systemic inflammation, and activation of the vascular endothelium.
evidence: This reflects established scientific knowledge about PARDS pathophysiology.

claim: Among nearly 400 children with pneumonia, an association was demonstrated between SFTPB Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and need for mechanical ventilation.
source: Among nearly 400 children with pneumonia, of whom the most severely affected had PARDS and need for mechanical ventilation, an association was demonstrated between SFTPB Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and need for mechanical ventilation (Dahmer et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dahmer et al., 2011, which reported this association.

claim: SNPs in SFTPA1, SFTPA2, and SFTPC were associated with acute respiratory failure and pulmonary dysfunction after hospital discharge in children.
source: In another study comparing children with acute respiratory failure and healthy newborn controls, SNPs in SFTPA1, SFTPA2, and SFTPC were associated with acute respiratory failure and pulmonary dysfunction after hospital discharge (Gandhi et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gandhi et al., 2020.

claim: The D allele of the ACE I/D variant is associated with increased ACE activity and higher ACE levels in plasma and tissue.
source: The insertion/deletion (I/D) variant (rs4646994, a 287–289 basepair Alu-type repeat sequence in intron 16) in the ACE1 gene has functional significance such that the D allele is associated with increased ACE activity and higher ACE levels in plasma and tissue.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about the functional significance of the ACE I/D variant.

claim: In children, the ACE I/D variant failed to demonstrate association with PARDS status but increased frequency of D allele was associated with PARDS severity.
source: In children, the I/D variant failed to demonstrate association with PARDS status but increased frequency of D allele was associated with PARDS severity (Cruces et al., 2012; Plunkett et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies examining the ACE I/D variant in pediatric ARDS.

claim: An adult study confirmed the association between the DD genotype, increased risk for ARDS, and increased mortality from ARDS.
source: An adult study confirmed the association between the DD genotype, increased risk for ARDS, and increased mortality from ARDS (Adamzik et al., 2007; Marshall et al., 2002) but did not test the I/D variant.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to adult ARDS studies.

claim: Adult ARDS mortality has been associated with two THBD (rs1042580 and rs3716123) and one PROCR (rs9574) SNPs.
source: Adult ARDS mortality has been associated with two THBD (rs1042580 and rs3716123) and one PROCR (rs9574) SNPs (Sapru et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sapru et al., 2016.

claim: In adults with sepsis, ANGPT2 intronic SNPs (rs2442608 and rs2442630) have been associated with increased susceptibility to acute lung injury (ALI).
source: In adults with sepsis, ANGPT2 intronic SNPs (rs2442608 and rs2442630) have been associated with increased susceptibility to acute lung injury (ALI) (Meyer et al., 2011) or ARDS across multiple cohorts (Su et al., 2009), one in which plasma ANGPT2 was implicated as a causal intermediate (Reilly et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies examining ANGPT2 SNPs in adult ALI/ARDS.

claim: ANGPT2 intronic SNPs have been associated with ARDS across multiple cohorts, with plasma ANGPT2 implicated as a causal intermediate in one study.
source: In adults with sepsis, ANGPT2 intronic SNPs (rs2442608 and rs2442630) have been associated with increased susceptibility to acute lung injury (ALI) (Meyer et al., 2011) or ARDS across multiple cohorts (Su et al., 2009), one in which plasma ANGPT2 was implicated as a causal intermediate (Reilly et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies, including one identifying a causal intermediate.

claim: In adults with trauma or sepsis as risk factors for ARDS, the development of ARDS was associated with ANGPT2.
source: In adults with trauma or sepsis as risk factors for ARDS, the development of ARDS was associated with ANGPT2 (Tejera et al., 2012) and blood type A in White patients (Reilly et al., 2021), potentially reflecting vascular inflammatory changes.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tejera et al., 2012.

claim: In adults with trauma or sepsis as risk factors for ARDS, the development of ARDS was associated with blood type A in White patients, potentially reflecting vascular inflammatory changes.
source: In adults with trauma or sepsis as risk factors for ARDS, the development of ARDS was associated with ANGPT2 (Tejera et al., 2012) and blood type A in White patients (Reilly et al., 2021), potentially reflecting vascular inflammatory changes.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reilly et al., 2021, with speculation about mechanism.

claim: An SNP in FLT1 (rs9513106) was associated with reduced susceptibility to ARDS in a cohort study involving adults of Spanish and Western European descent with sepsis.
source: An SNP in FLT1 (rs9513106) was associated with reduced susceptibility to ARDS in a cohort study involving adults of Spanish and Western European descent with sepsis (Hernandez-Pacheco et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hernandez-Pacheco et al., 2018.

claim: Candidate gene studies have demonstrated associations between the development of ARDS in patients with clinical risk factors and polymorphisms implicated in pulmonary inflammation, systemic inflammation, or endothelial activation.
source: As a whole, candidate gene studies have demonstrated associations between the development of ARDS in patients with clinical risk factors and polymorphisms implicated in pulmonary inflammation, systemic inflammation, or endothelial activation.
evidence: This is a summary statement drawing on the cited candidate gene studies discussed in the preceding text.

claim: The association of specific SNPs with ARDS has not been adequately replicated, and pediatric studies have been few.
source: However, the association of specific SNPs with ARDS has not been adequately replicated, and pediatric studies have been few.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the literature based on the review conducted.

claim: Notable disadvantages of candidate gene studies are false positives and poor replication.
source: Notable disadvantages of candidate gene studies are false positives and poor replication.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about limitations of candidate gene study methodology.

claim: Candidate gene studies may unduly emphasize known biological themes while failing to address what has not yet been hypothesized.
source: Furthermore, candidate gene studies are hypothesis-driven, investigating only genes of interest based on prior knowledge, and thus may unduly emphasize known biological themes while failing to address what has not yet been hypothesized.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of hypothesis-driven approaches.

claim: Early increase in endothelial biomarkers ANGPT2 and ANGPT2/ANGPT1 ratio was associated with the development of PARDS in children with extrapulmonary sepsis.
source: Early increase in endothelial biomarkers ANGPT2 and ANGPT2/ANGPT1 ratio was associated with the development of PARDS in our prior study of children with extrapulmonary sepsis (Whitney et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Whitney et al., 2020b.

claim: Among children with PARDS, persistent organ dysfunction or death was associated with rapid decline in endothelial biomarker sFLT, and slow decline in von Willebrand Factor (vWF) and TM.
source: Among those with PARDS, persistent organ dysfunction or death was associated with rapid decline in endothelial biomarker sFLT, and slow decline in von Willebrand Factor (vWF) and TM, which reflect the activation of the coagulation system (Whitney et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Whitney et al., 2020b.

claim: In children who underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplant, PARDS mortality was associated with both early elevation in and subsequent increase of ANGPT2.
source: In a cohort of children, who underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplant, PARDS mortality was associated with both early elevation in and subsequent increase of ANGPT2 (Zinter et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zinter et al., 2016.

claim: A profile of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) associated with multiple markers of inflammation and endothelial activation predicted severe morbidity or mortality in a cohort of 235 children with PARDS.
source: A profile of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) associated with multiple markers of inflammation and endothelial activation and predicted severe morbidity or mortality in a cohort of 235 children with PARDS (Zinter et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zinter et al., 2019.

claim: One adult ALI study confirmed the association between increased ANGTP2 and mortality, modified by the presence of infection.
source: One study of adults with ALI (Supplementary file 1) confirmed the association between increased ANGTP2 and mortality, modified by the presence of infection (Calfee et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Calfee et al., 2012.

claim: In a cohort of children with acute respiratory failure, circulating interleukin-8 (IL-8) level was associated with worse outcomes but not PARDS status.
source: In a cohort of children with acute respiratory failure, circulating interleukin-8 (IL-8) level was associated with worse outcomes but not PARDS status (Flori et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Flori et al., 2019.

claim: The association of IL-8 with poor outcome from PARDS in the context of sepsis was confirmed in a larger cohort.
source: The association of IL-8 with poor outcome from PARDS in the context of sepsis was confirmed in a larger cohort (Yehya and Wong, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yehya and Wong, 2018.

claim: Increased RAGE and ANGPT2 are associated with nonsurvival and increased number of nonpulmonary organ failures in PARDS.
source: Yehya et al. found increased RAGE and ANGPT2 to be associated with nonsurvival and increased number of nonpulmonary organ failures in PARDS (Yehya et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yehya et al., 2016.

claim: Three studies of septic adults supported the association between increased RAGE and ARDS status.
source: Three studies of septic adults (Supplementary file 1) supported these findings in demonstrating the association between increased RAGE and ARDS status (Uchida et al., 2006; Jones et al., 2020; Ware et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three adult ARDS studies.

claim: Endotypes of PARDS have been identified, which are associated with distinct clinical factors and outcomes, potentially reflecting differences in pathobiology.
source: Distinguishing endophenotypes has been of interest in ARDS, and endotypes of PARDS have been identified, which are associated with distinct clinical factors and outcomes (Yehya et al., 2018; Whitney et al., 2020a; Yehya et al., 2018) potentially reflecting differences in pathobiology (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies identifying PARDS endotypes.

claim: Wong et al. used a large panel of biomarkers to define endotypes in pediatric sepsis, which were associated with differential mortality and response to therapies, including steroids.
source: First, Wong et al. used a large panel of biomarkers to define endotypes in pediatric sepsis, which were associated with differential mortality and response to therapies, including steroids (Wong et al., 2015; Wong et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wong et al., 2015 and 2012.

claim: Yehya et al. used similar methods to define an endotype associated with poor outcomes from acute hypoxemic respiratory failure in septic children, identified by IL-8, C-C chemokine ligand 3 (CCL3), and heat shock protein 70 kDa 1B (HSPA1B), and age.
source: Yehya et al., 2019, recognizing sepsis as the most common cause of PARDS, used similar methods to define an endotype associated with poor outcomes from acute hypoxemic respiratory failure in septic children, identified by IL-8, C-C chemokine ligand 3 (CCL3), and heat shock protein 70 kDa 1B (HSPA1B), and age.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yehya et al., 2019.

claim: The identifying characteristics of the endotype defined by Yehya et al. were tested in a PARDS cohort with good prediction of mortality.
source: The identifying characteristics were then tested in a PARDS cohort with good prediction of mortality (Yehya and Wong, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yehya and Wong, 2018.

claim: Elevation in endothelial biomarkers ANGPT2/ANGPT1 ratio, VCAM1, and vWF distinguished children with ARDS due to indirect compared to direct lung injury.
source: We previously reported that elevation in endothelial biomarkers ANGPT2/ANGPT1 ratio, VCAM1, and vWF distinguished children with ARDS due to indirect (e.g., extrapulmonary sepsis or trauma, shock, transfusion, pancreatitis) compared to direct (e.g., pneumonia, aspiration, drowning) lung injury (Whitney et al., 2020a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Whitney et al., 2020a.

claim: An adult ARDS study showed lower ANGPT2 and higher SP-D in those with direct lung injury.
source: An adult ARDS study with complementary results (Supplementary file 1) showed lower ANGPT2 and higher SP-D in those with direct lung injury (Calfee et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Calfee et al., 2015.

claim: Biomarkers reflecting systemic inflammation and endothelial activation have been associated with worse clinical outcomes in adult ARDS with a differential response to therapies.
source: Biomarkers reflecting systemic inflammation and endothelial activation have been associated with worse clinical outcomes in adult ARDS (Supplementary file 1) with a differential response to therapies (Bos et al., 2017; Calfee et al., 2014; Famous et al., 2017; Sinha et al., 2020; Sinha et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to adult ARDS studies.

claim: Grunwell et al. examined neutrophils from children with PARDS secondary to viral lower respiratory tract infection with or without bacterial pneumonia, examining transmigration through their model airway with cell-free tracheal aspirate fluid.
source: Grunwell et al. examined neutrophils from children with PARDS secondary to viral lower respiratory tract infection with or without bacterial pneumonia, examining transmigration through their model airway with cell-free tracheal aspirate fluid (Grunwell et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Grunwell et al., 2019.

claim: Patients with bacterial pneumonia had neutrophils with increased markers of activation and a defective respiratory burst, with airway fluid containing higher MPO and NE activity and decreased killing of H. influenzae and S. aureus.
source: Patients with bacterial pneumonia had neutrophils with increased markers of activation and a defective respiratory burst, with airway fluid containing higher MPO and NE activity and decreased killing of H. influenzae and S. aureus (Grunwell et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Grunwell et al., 2019.

claim: In a follow-up study comparing tracheal aspirates from intubated children with and without pediatric ARDS, increased type I interferon signaling (increased phosphorylation of STAT1), increased NET release were observed.
source: In a follow-up study comparing tracheal aspirates from intubated children with and without pediatric ARDS, increased type I interferon signaling (increased phosphorylation of STAT1), increased NET release (Grunwell et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Grunwell et al., 2021.

claim: Increased markers of neutrophil activation and degranulation were observed in children with PARDS, also associated with fewer ventilator days in patients with higher airway NE.
source: Increased markers of neutrophil activation and degranulation were observed in children with PARDS, also associated with fewer ventilator days in patients with higher airway NE (Grunwell et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Grunwell et al., 2021.

claim: Similar findings were documented in lower airway neutrophils and neutrophils exposed to airway fluid from adults with vs. without ARDS, including decreased apoptosis and macrophage activity and increased NET formation in ARDS.
source: Similar findings were documented in lower airway neutrophils and neutrophils exposed to airway fluid from adults with vs. without ARDS (Supplementary file 1), including decreased apoptosis and macrophage activity and increased NET formation in ARDS (Grégoire et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Grégoire et al., 2018.

claim: In a multiphase study using GWAS to compare European-American adults with trauma-associated ALI to controls, ALI was associated with rs47191 in the PPFIA1 gene.
source: In a multiphase study using GWAS to compare European-American adults with trauma-associated ALI to controls, ALI was associated with rs47191 in the PPFIA1 gene, which encodes liprin-α-1, a protein involved in cell–matrix interactions and cell adhesion (Christie et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Christie et al., 2012.

claim: A study of African American patients with ARDS compared to at-risk controls found ARDS to be associated with a coding SNP (rs2228315) in the SELPLG gene.
source: A study of African American patients with ARDS compared to at-risk controls found ARDS to be associated with and a coding SNP (rs2228315) in the SELPLG gene, which regulates neutrophil adherence and diapedesis across the vascular endothelium (Bime et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bime et al., 2018.

claim: SELPLG knockout mice showed significantly reduced LPS-induced inflammatory lung injury compared with wild-type mice, and a neutralizing antibody against PSGL-1 reduced lung inflammation.
source: SELPLG knockout mice showed significantly reduced LPS-induced inflammatory lung injury compared with wild-type mice, and a neutralizing antibody against PSGL-1 (P-selectin glycoprotein ligand 1) reduced lung inflammation.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from the same study (Bime et al., 2018) mentioned in the preceding sentence.

claim: In a comparison of European adults with ARDS and at-risk septic patients, an SNP in FLT1 was associated with reduced susceptibility to ARDS.
source: In a comparison of European adults with ARDS and at-risk septic patients, an SNP in FLT1 was associated with reduced susceptibility to ARDS (Guillen-Guio et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Guillen-Guio et al., 2020.

claim: Sample sizes required for case and control groups in GWAS are large relative to the prevalence of ARDS.
source: First, sample sizes required for case and control groups are large relative to the prevalence of ARDS.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about GWAS methodology requirements.

claim: Biological interpretation of risk alleles and understanding their relationship to associated genes in disease development is challenging in GWAS.
source: Second, biological interpretation of risk alleles and understanding their relationship to associated genes in disease development is challenging.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about limitations of GWAS interpretation.

claim: In evaluating a cohort of children with sepsis and acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, Yehya et al. identified two distinct transcriptomic profiles differentially associated with mortality and persistent organ dysfunction.
source: In evaluating a cohort of children with sepsis and acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, Yehya et al. identified two distinct transcriptomic profiles differentially associated with mortality and persistent organ dysfunction (Yehya et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yehya et al., 2019.

claim: Yehya et al. evaluated a cohort of PARDS patients using peripheral blood transcriptome to identify three subgroups that were associated with distinct baseline clinical characteristics and ARDS outcomes.
source: Subsequently, the same group evaluated a cohort of PARDS patients using peripheral blood transcriptome to identify three subgroups that were associated with distinct baseline clinical characteristics and ARDS outcomes (Yehya et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yehya et al., 2020.

claim: The first subgroup identified by Yehya et al. was characterized by enriched adaptive immune response and persistent hypoxemia.
source: The first subgroup was characterized by enriched adaptive immune response and persistent hypoxemia.
evidence: This describes findings from Yehya et al., 2020 mentioned in the preceding sentence.

claim: The second subgroup identified by Yehya et al. was characterized by the activation of complement-related pathways.
source: The second subgroup was characterized by the activation of complement-related pathways, and the third exhibited suppression of adaptive immune and T-cell receptor pathways, which was associated with improved survival.
evidence: This describes findings from Yehya et al., 2020 mentioned in the preceding sentence.

claim: The third subgroup identified by Yehya et al. exhibited suppression of adaptive immune and T-cell receptor pathways, which was associated with improved survival.
source: The second subgroup was characterized by the activation of complement-related pathways, and the third exhibited suppression of adaptive immune and T-cell receptor pathways, which was associated with improved survival.
evidence: This describes findings from Yehya et al., 2020 mentioned in the preceding sentence.

claim: Grunwell et al. collected tracheal aspirate samples from 28 patients with PARDS and 24 without PARDS to discover transcriptomic signature in airway cells.
source: To discover transcriptomic signature in airway cells, Grunwell et al., 2021 collected tracheal aspirate samples from 28 patients with PARDS and 24 without PARDS.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Grunwell et al., 2021.

claim: The top-ranked gene in the primary airway cells from Grunwell et al.'s study was IL17A, and a 62-gene prediction model for PARDS was developed, which was enriched with the genes in cytokine–cytokine receptor interaction.
source: The top-ranked gene in the primary airway cells was IL17A, and a 62-gene prediction model for PARDS was developed, which was enriched with the genes in cytokine–cytokine receptor interaction.
evidence: This describes findings from Grunwell et al., 2021 mentioned in the preceding sentence.

claim: The most significantly altered gene in the neutrophil reporter assay from Grunwell et al.'s study was NT5E.
source: A neutrophil reporter assay was used to monitor gene expression changes seen in healthy donor neutrophils exposed to airway fluid patients with and without ARDS. The most significantly altered gene in the neutrophil reporter assay was NT5E.
evidence: This describes findings from Grunwell et al., 2021 mentioned in the preceding sentence.

claim: Rogers et al. used an untargeted metabolomics platform to compare the profile of pulmonary edema fluid collected at the time of endotracheal intubation for 16 adults with ARDS compared to 13 with cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
source: Recently, Rogers et al. used an untargeted metabolomics platform to compare the profile of pulmonary edema fluid collected at the time of endotracheal intubation for 16 adults with ARDS compared to 13 with cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rogers et al., 2017.

claim: Rogers et al. found a high metabolite endotype characterized by higher concentration of lipids, amino acids, and carbohydrates to be associated with higher mortality from ARDS.
source: They found a high metabolite endotype characterized by higher concentration of lipids, amino acids, and carbohydrates to be associated with higher mortality from ARDS (Rogers et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rogers et al., 2017.

claim: Of the 735 GP associations initially found from the NHGRI-EBI GWAS catalog, 140 GP associations were selected from studies with 3000 or more individuals in both initial and replication cohort.
source: Of the 735 GP associations initially found from catalog, we selected 140 GP associations from studies with 3000 or more individuals in both initial and replication cohort.
evidence: This describes the authors' analysis of the GWAS catalog data.

claim: The 140 selected GP pairs involved 32 candidate genes and 64 distinct traits.
source: The 140 selected GP pairs involved 32 candidate genes and 64 distinct traits (defined as having distinct identifier in Experimental Factor Ontology [https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ols/ontologies/efo]).
evidence: This describes the authors' analysis of the GWAS catalog data.

claim: The network of associations between genes and simplified phenotypes confirms that the candidate genes are mostly associated with key phenotypes of ARDS: cardiovascular disease, pulmonary function, and systemic inflammatory diseases.
source: The network of associations between genes and simplified phenotypes confirms that the candidate genes are mostly associated with key phenotypes of ARDS: cardiovascular disease, pulmonary function, and systemic inflammatory diseases (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the authors' analysis of GWAS catalog data and presented in Figure 1.

claim: Genetic pleiotropy may exist between individuals with higher risk for ARDS and clinical phenotypes including cardiovascular disease, pulmonary function, and systemic inflammatory diseases.
source: Genetic pleiotropy may exist between individuals with higher risk for ARDS and these clinical phenotypes.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed associations.

claim: Increased ANGPT2 has been proposed to have a causal role in ARDS due to endothelial activation.
source: Therefore, increased ANGPT2 has been proposed to have a causal role in ARDS due to endothelial activation (Reilly et al., 2018) and ANGPT or ANGPT2/1 levels associate with clinical outcome (Whitney et al., 2020a; Whitney et al., 2020b; Zinter et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reilly et al., 2018.

claim: ANGPT or ANGPT2/1 levels associate with clinical outcome in ARDS.
source: Therefore, increased ANGPT2 has been proposed to have a causal role in ARDS due to endothelial activation (Reilly et al., 2018) and ANGPT or ANGPT2/1 levels associate with clinical outcome (Whitney et al., 2020a; Whitney et al., 2020b; Zinter et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Patients may present to care in different phases of ARDS.
source: When considering pathobiological evolution of ARDS through these proposed phases, it is important to note that (1) patients may present to care in different phases, (2) patients may progress through phases at different rates, and (3) scientific knowledge of ARDS phases is more developed for adults than children.
evidence: This reflects clinical knowledge about ARDS presentation.

claim: Patients may progress through ARDS phases at different rates.
source: When considering pathobiological evolution of ARDS through these proposed phases, it is important to note that (1) patients may present to care in different phases, (2) patients may progress through phases at different rates, and (3) scientific knowledge of ARDS phases is more developed for adults than children.
evidence: This reflects clinical knowledge about ARDS progression.

claim: Scientific knowledge of ARDS phases is more developed for adults than children.
source: When considering pathobiological evolution of ARDS through these proposed phases, it is important to note that (1) patients may present to care in different phases, (2) patients may progress through phases at different rates, and (3) scientific knowledge of ARDS phases is more developed for adults than children.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of scientific knowledge.

claim: Risk alleles for ARDS are reported in SFTPB and EGF genes that are important for homeostatic function of AT1 cells.
source: Risk alleles for ARDS are reported in SFTPB and EGF genes that are important homeostatic function of AT1 cells.
evidence: This summarizes findings from candidate gene studies discussed earlier in the manuscript.

claim: In the exudative phase, injured AT1 cells release soluble RAGE, SP-B, SP-D, CC-16 (SCGB1A), lamininγ2 (LAMC2), KL-6 (MUC1), and KGF (FGF7).
source: In the exudative phase, injured AT1 cells release soluble RAGE, SP-B, SP-D, CC-16 (SCGB1A), lamininγ2 (LAMC2), KL-6 (MUC1), and KGF (FGF7, Figure 2, panel B).
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about ARDS pathophysiology and is illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: In the proliferative phase, TGF-β and PDGF are released from AT2 cells.
source: In the proliferative phase, TGF-β and PDGF are released from AT2 cells (Figure 2, panel C).
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about ARDS pathophysiology and is illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Activated AT2 cells continue to secrete TGF-β, PDGF, and IGF-1 to promote interstitial and intraalveolar fibrosis, which restrict lung capacity.
source: Activated AT2 cells continue to secrete TGF-β, PDGF, and IGF-1 to promote interstitial and intraalveolar fibrosis, which restrict lung capacity (Figure 2, panel D).
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about ARDS pathophysiology and is illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Genetic susceptibility to ARDS has been reported for genes that are highly expressed in endothelial cells and have functional significance for normal cellular function, including ANGPT2, TIE2, ACE, PBEF, VEGF, and PAI1.
source: Genetic susceptibility to ARDS has been reported for the genes that are highly expressed in endothelial cells and have functional significance for normal cellular function, including ANGPT2 (ANGPT2), TIE2 (TEK), ACE, PBEF (NAMPT), VEGF (VEGFA), and PAI1 (SERPINE1) (Acosta-Herrera et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Acosta-Herrera et al., 2014.

claim: Protein biomarkers released from injured endothelial cells include ANGPT1, ANGPT2, VEGF, vWF, apolipoproteins, cell-free hemoglobin, PAI1, endothelial glycocalyx, sTM, sICAM, and PROC.
source: Protein biomarkers released from injured endothelial cells include ANGPT1, ANGPT2, VEGF, vWF, apolipoproteins, cell-free hemoglobin, PAI1, endothelial glycocalyx, sTM (THBD), sICAM (ICAM1), and PROC (Figure 2, panel B).
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about endothelial injury biomarkers and is illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Alveolar macrophages are transformed to inflammatory M1-like macrophages by the activation of NF-κB signaling pathway then cytokines and chemokines, including TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, CCL2, and CCL7, are released to recruit neutrophils in the exudative phase.
